words.intro: At 2,962 metres, the Zugspitze is the highest point in Germany. You can reach it by train, then cable car, then a few steps, and you can buy a beer at the top.

grammar[0].fact: Germany’s highest railway, the *Zugspitzbahn*, opened in 1930 and climbs through a long tunnel. The cable car on the Austrian side went up earlier, and the rivalry between the two villages is still taken personally.

opener.caption: Auf der Zugspitze: höher geht es in Deutschland nicht.
reading.intro: Lena, Max and Maya have gone up the Zugspitze. Max comes from England, and he has spent the whole trip asking whose country has the biggest, oldest and longest of everything. At the top, in the café, Frau Huber’s cousin Toni runs the till.
reading.photos[0].caption: Die Zugspitzbahn: Mit dem Zug in den Berg.
reading.photos[1].caption: Auf dem Gipfel: Antennen, ein Café und ein sehr teurer Kaffee.
reading.en: Max: This is the highest mountain in Germany, yes? But the mountains in Austria are higher. · Lena: And in England? What’s your highest mountain called? · Max: Scafell Pike. Nine hundred metres. But it’s the most beautiful. · Maya: What do you like drinking best, Max? It’s on me. · Toni: Hello. The coffee here is the highest coffee in Germany. And the most expensive. Seven euros. · Max: Seven euros! That’s the most expensive coffee I’ve ever seen. · Toni: But you have the best view. It’s best to look south. Austria’s over there, and the coffee is even dearer there. · Maya: Is that the best weather you’ve ever had? · Toni: This is the worst. Yesterday we could see forty kilometres. Today you can see me. · A cloud comes in at the window. Max silently drinks the highest, most expensive and coldest coffee in Germany. · Max: In England, the coffee is the worst. But it only costs three pounds.
reading.fact: The summit of the Zugspitze is on the German-Austrian border, and there is no fence: you can go from one country to the other through the café. The peak is getting less icy every year: its glaciers are expected to be gone within the decade, and Germany has only a few left.

document.caption: Ein Gipfelbuch: Was steht darin?
document.intro: The first page of a real summit book, kept in a metal box on a mountain in Saxony. Walkers write their names in it. This page, in old type, is a poem with four rules for them. Two of its words are superlatives.
document.fact: Summit books are a real German tradition: nearly every peak in the Alps has one, in a tin at the foot of the cross. You sign, write the date, say something about the weather, and someone may read it twenty years later.
